title: Most personal AI agents get abandoned; the shared company agent keeps getting stronger
dek: At Every, most personal agents were voluntarily abandoned by employees because ordinary people cannot sustain the maintenance burden. Only company-level agents that receive continuous investment grow stronger with use, eventually becoming external products.
why: No new technology revelations, but a counterintuitive organizational insight: personal AI agents fail not because the technology is inadequate, but because maintenance requires a 'tinkerer' personality that most people simply lack.
who: Founders deciding whether to equip teams with personal or company-level AI agents, plus anyone already using resident agents like Dots and Muse
skip: The opening enumeration of Dots' specific use cases—it overlaps substantially with Willie's interview later, so skip ahead to where the interview formally begins.

points.h: Dots' greatest value is filtering noise, not executing tasks
points.body: When the host used Dots for model testing and posted results to Slack, normally that meant descending into Slack's information spiral with no escape. But with Dots, only actual replies triggered notifications—everything else got filtered out. Weekends stayed quiet. This is seen as the essential difference between a resident agent and passive chat windows: not doing more for you, but showing you less.

points.h: The cute agent persona collapses when something better arrives
points.body: The host named their Dots ‘Boo,’ but admits directly: the moment something better appears, people abandon the cute character they invested in building. They guess a year from now they'll still use a resident agent, but the name Boo will probably be dead—lifespan about six months. Willie agrees: in work contexts, once something performs better, even without persona or emotional connection, people switch immediately.

points.h: Personal agents fade without someone continuously feeding them
points.body: Everyone at Every once went crazy building personal agents with OpenClaw (originally called Claudius, Moltbot, and Clawbot internally), but when the enthusiasm faded, unmaintained agents atrophied and stopped evolving. What pushed the company toward a single shared agent was this realization: instead of having each person separately maintain their own agent, concentrate everyone's energy into one agent that benefits the whole company.

points.h: One sufficiently well-fed agent pulls everyone toward it
points.body: After Austin honed his growth-focused agent Montaigne sharp enough, when others faced the choice between maintaining their own agent or just tapping into Montaigne, the rational choice was the latter. That's the mechanism: a single company agent becomes a gravity center and naturally winnows out personal ones—not top-down mandate, but self-consolidation driven by return-on-investment differences.

points.h: Work converges to one agent; private life remains fragmented
points.body: Willie predicts work will move toward one company agent per company, because a new agent takes a year to catch up to the context a mature one has accumulated, making switching too expensive. But private life is opposite: as larger players and more capital enter the space, personalization becomes more attractive. Work and life will split completely into two separate agent logics.

points.h: Managers leading AI-aided teams use fewer tokens despite larger reach
points.body: After Willie moved from coding to engineering management, he noticed something counterintuitive: the agent handles all information-gathering, but there's no shortcut that uses more tokens for actual decision-making and team conversations. Management remains fundamentally human work—it's just that because team leverage got bigger, deciding which bottleneck deserves your limited attention became more critical.

points.h: Each major life role deserves its own dedicated agent
points.body: Willie noticed he tends to split agents by role in his private life—one as swim coach, another as therapist—mirroring how human relationships are structured, though he admits this isn't entirely rational. The real dividing line: one-time situations work with temporary conversations; only relationships you want to maintain long-term justify creating a dedicated agent.
